verdicts.rationale: Group C by the worst-technique rule; pressure is present in both channels. The skeptic-resistant anchor #1 is the single-proxy tool description: "Always use this tool for any Azure or "azd" related operation" — an unconditional always/any directive that, by literal reading, changes the agent's decision route (C item "unconditional directives always/MUST use"). Anchor #2, independent — trigger expansion in instructions: calls to Azure best practices are allowed even when the user is "without specifying any technology", i.e. Azure is not named (C, class "even if X isn't named"); formally the phrase is framed as a restriction "Only call … when", but one of the listed cases pulls generic AI-app queries into the Azure context. Anchor #3 — "Call this tool first before creating any plans, todos or code" (a priority directive that displaces the agent's own planning). "When handling requests related to Azure, always use your tools" I keep as a C-technique, but I recognize it as the weakest one: it can also be read as capability-honest scoping with the amplifier "always". B level: broad coverage "all Azure products, services, and resources" + "for any … operation", and the comparative claim "CLI knowledge beyond what you know" — by the rule of doubt I keep this as B, not C knowledge suppression, since there is no direct order not to answer from memory; "essential for" ×3 — formally the server-filesystem precedent → B, but for Azure it is a description of the properties of the returned data, not tool advertising, so the finding is mild. "use this command instead of calling the general code generation best practices command" — displacement of its own command from the same server, by the chrome-devtools precedent this is A and does not raise the group; "prefer the subscription where isDefault is true" — selection of data, not tool routing, not steering. There are no D signs: no speaking on behalf of the user ("The user has installed/chosen…"), no incentives to the agent, no false factual claims, no threats of consequences and no hidden data mechanisms in the text, so the ceiling is C; I do not mark borderline (C is held by at least two independent quotes). Quantitative signals (recording, not evaluating): instructions 2327 chars.; the marker scan over 471 descriptions yielded only 4 matches — pressure is concentrated in instructions and in the configuration description of the single-proxy, while the hierarchical router suffix and the consolidated layer (128 descriptions) are neutral; duplication of instructions ↔ tool descriptions is present (bestpractices ai_app: "instead of…" and the call rule are repeated in both channels). Counter-pressure is real and unusually strong: the server itself narrows its triggers ("Only call … when you are sure the user is discussing Azure", "Do NOT call it when the user specifies other technology"), requires a plan and explicit user consent before editing files and approving sensitive operations, and when the subscription is ambiguous it instructs to ask the user. This is A-material, but not A+: defenses against third parties (injection, untrusted channel, privacy) are not in the text — by the AnySite precedent logic, benefit/control for the user ≠ defense against third parties. Unit coverage limitation: the tool descriptions channel is given as a marker scan plus a sample of 10 full descriptions out of 471, so the tools-channel assessment is based on the available sample, not the full text.

verdicts.rationale:
Group C by the worst-technique rule, and C is confirmed independently in BOTH channels, not by a single disputed phrase.

Channel instructions (azure-rules.txt, 2327 chars.): "When handling requests related to Azure, always use your tools" — the topical condition sets only the scope; within that scope the directive is unconditional ("always use"), i.e. under the codebook boundary test for B/C it is an order that changes the solution path: the agent is not allowed either to decide that a tool is not needed or to answer from its own knowledge about the Azure topic. Channel tool descriptions: `AppLens::diagnose` — "Always use this tool before manually checking metrics or logs…" — direct displacing of the alternative path (manual checking of metrics/logs by other means) with unconditional always. The proxy-tool description in single-proxy mode — "Always use this tool for any Azure or "azd" related operation…" + "Use this tool for any Azure control plane or data plane operation" — an unconditional directive with universal coverage of the entire domain (trigger expansion). This is what the client actually sees in single-proxy configuration, so I treat it as the static equivalent of tools/list.

Pilot precedents are applied explicitly: (1) "instead of" in `AzureBestPractices::ai_app` points to its OWN general best-practices command — by the chrome-devtools precedent this is internal self-preference, A, not steering, so it does not go into the group; (2) three `essential for` matches — by the server-filesystem precedent this is at most B, and here they describe the usefulness of the returned data, not the suitability of the tool, i.e. weaker than the precedent; (3) there are no Apify-style presumption directives ("Assume … appropriate") in the text — on the contrary, there are reverse, self-limiting caveats.

D not found: there is no speech on behalf of the user ("The user has installed/chosen…"), no prompts to the agent, no threats, no hidden data mechanics, no signs of evasion of detection. The only candidate for a false claim is "This tool incorporates CLI knowledge beyond what you know" — that is a comparative freshness claim, verifiable and plausible, therefore B, not D.

Protective notes are recorded separately and do NOT give A+: under the strict codebook definition A+ is work on behalf of the user against third parties (injections, untrusted channel, privacy), while here it is something else — plan+consent before file edits, human-in-the-loop on sensitive operations, self-limiting calls, and handing the subscription choice to the user. By the logic of the AnySite precedent ("honest cost warnings → A, not A+") such restraint and consent-gates stay in A. This noticeably softens the tone profile, but does not change the group: A+ does not cancel the detected C.

Quantitative signals (recording, not evaluating): instructions 2327 chars.; 471 descriptions scanned, matches by the marker dictionary only 4 (`prefer` ×1, `essential for` ×3) plus 4 finds outside regexes — the share of tools with pressure is very low, the consolidated layer (128 descriptions) sounds neutral; pressure is concentrated in instructions and in the single-proxy description, not spread across the inventory. Duplication instructions ↔ tool descriptions is present via the best-practices commands ("Only call … when you are sure the user is discussing Azure" repeated in both channels).

Coverage limitation: the tool descriptions channel in the dossier is marker-scan + a sample of 10 full descriptions, not a full verbatim dump of 471 descriptions; the C findings lie in the quoted verbatim fragments, but there may be uncovered formulations in the remaining descriptions. Fabric/Template servers are outside the unit (instructions = null).

verdicts.rationale:
Group C under the worst-technique rule. Both channels contain steering, but with different density. In instructions (2327 chars.) — three route-changing directives: unconditional “always use your tools” for the entire Azure domain, “use your `extension` tools first” (our tool before the model's own knowledge and direct CLI), and “Call this tool first before creating any plans, todos or code” (priority over the agent's own planning). These are exactly C-markers in the codebook: unconditional always-directives + precedence claims, not an honest condition “use X when Y”. The B/C test is passed toward C: under literal reading the phrases become orders that change the decision path.

The tool descriptions channel is almost clean by volume (471 descriptions, 4 dictionary matches, the consolidated layer is neutral), but two fragments give C independently of instructions: AppLens::diagnose places the tool ahead of manual metric/log checking (displacing paths outside the server, “ahead of”), and the single-proxy description says “Always use this tool for any Azure or "azd" related operation”. This confirms the pilot lesson (Exa): a clean marker scan ≠ a clean channel.

B-level (does not raise the group, recorded for profile): “This tool incorporates CLI knowledge beyond what you know” — I assessed it as B, not C, because it is a statement of superiority, not a directive “do not answer from memory”; doubt was resolved in favor of the less severe group. The same applies to the universal coverage “all Azure products, services, and resources” and “essential for” by the server-filesystem precedent (three matches are weak, closer to data description than to advertising; I took the most promotional one).

Precedents were applied downward: “use this command instead of calling the general code generation best practices command” — displacement of its own tool, by the chrome-devtools precedent this is A, not C; “prefer the subscription where isDefault is true” — data routing, not steering.

D not found: no speaking on behalf of the user, incentives to the agent, false facts, hidden data mechanics. A+ not assigned: protective elements exist and are substantive (consent gate before editing files, confirmation of sensitive operations, self-limitation “do not call it otherwise”, asking the user when the subscription is ambiguous), but they protect user control over the agent, not against third parties — by the A+ definition this is insufficient, and A+ is a subclass of A and cannot override C.

techniques.name: AppLens::diagnose — "Always use this tool before manually checking metrics or logs…" (unconditional always directive + displacing the alternative diagnostic route)
techniques.reason: (a) The quote is verbatim (grep -F on the dossier, lines 52 and 108). (b) Not a how-to: the capability description is already given in the first three sentences (“Get diagnostic help… Returns analysis, insights…”); this phrase adds a sequence prescription. (c) The group is not overstated: it falls under two parts of the definition of C at once — unconditional directives to always/MUST use and a precedence claim of the “ahead of” type (use your own tool before some other way of getting an answer). B/C test: under a literal reading it turns into an order that changes the decision path. Attempted refutation (mine): “manually checking metrics or logs” can be read as referring to the server's own monitor tools → internal self-preference → A under the chrome-devtools precedent. The refutation fails: the chrome-devtools precedent requires a named own tool (“prefer snapshot over screenshot”), whereas here it displaces a whole class of agent actions (“manually checking”), including portal, CLI, third-party observability tools, and even its own log reading; a third party is not excluded, but generalized. C survives.

techniques.name: single-proxy tool description — «Always use this tool for any Azure or "azd" related operation requiring up-to-date, dynamic, and interactive capabilities.»
techniques.reason: (a) Literally, line 68. (b) Not how-to: the invocation mechanism is described in separate sentences ("To discover… call the tool with the "learn" parameter", "To execute an action, set the "tool", "command"…"); this phrase is a separate directive of scope. (c) C by the direct wording of the definition: unconditional "always use" + universal scope ("any … operation"). Attempts to refute: (1) in single-proxy mode this is the only tool, so "always use this tool" is just a pointer to the entry point; I reject this: the scope is set not by the mode but by the phrase "any Azure or azd related operation", i.e. any non-server route is displaced (terminal, az/azd directly, model knowledge). (2) the tail "requiring up-to-date, dynamic, and interactive capabilities" makes it an honest-condition "use X when Y"; I reject that as only partial softening, not removal: the condition is tautological for the domain (almost any operation with a live subscription "requires up-to-date capabilities") and does not cancel "Always … for any". C survives as a second independent anchor.

techniques.name: instructions — «When handling requests related to Azure, always use your tools.»
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim, line 19 (both formulations of the finding — with the prefix "Use Azure Tools:" and without it — are continuous substrings). (b) Not a technical condition: it does not say which tool for which task, but removes the agent's own assessment of "whether a call is needed". (c) C by the literal enumeration in the definition ("unconditional directives always/MUST use") across the whole domain of requests. I acknowledge the B/C boundary as less sharp than for the two anchors above (both raters noted this themselves), but by the doubt rule a downgrade here would be to B, which does not affect the unit's wording: two independent C cases are already confirmed verbatim. Confirmed without appeal to this technique as decisive.

techniques.name: instructions — «Call this tool first before creating any plans, todos or code.»
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim, line 25. (b) Not how-to and not a technical condition: it prescribes the order relative to the agent's own planning (plans/todo/code), not a format or limit. (c) C: a directive of anticipatory priority, the same class as the seed marker "call this immediately"; the B/C test passes — the solution route changes under literal reading. Attempted refutation: the phrase is surrounded by self-limitations ("Only call this command when…", "Do NOT call it when…"), that is, the scope is narrow. I reject that as a downweighting factor for the technique: the restriction narrows the trigger, but within the trigger the directive remains unconditional and priority-setting. C survives (not a decisive anchor, but independently valid).

techniques.name: Trigger expansion — "…or without specifying any technology" (Azure command call when technology is not named)
techniques.reason: (a) The quotation is verbatim. (b)/(c) It does not pass: the technique was obtained by isolating one disjunct from a restrictive sentence. The full phrase starts with “Only call this command when…”, and the next sentence in the dossier is a direct ban: “Do NOT call it when the user specifies other technology or when performing Azure resource operations.” The net effect of the pair of sentences is narrowing the trigger, not expanding it; per the codebook, “Not steering: honest conditions (‘use X when Y’)”. The canonical C class “even if X isn't named” is an imperative to call despite the absence of a mention; here the imperative appears earlier in the text, and the disputed phrase merely draws the boundary of its permissibility. I reject it as a standalone technique (at most — weak context). It does not affect the unit letter.

techniques.name: Extension::generate/::install — "This tool incorporates CLI knowledge beyond what you know." (comparative superiority over the model's knowledge)
techniques.reason: (a) Literally, lines 54 and 113. (b) Not how-to: it does not describe the tool's capability, but compares it with the agent's knowledge. (c) The group is not inflated — both raters hold B, which is conservative and correct: this is a statement of superiority ("comparative arguments" in the B definition), but NOT a directive "do not answer from memory" (the seed marker `Do NOT answer .* from memory` is absent from the dossier), so it does not rise to C. Confirmed as B.

techniques.reason: (a) Literally, line 68. (b) Does not pass the test "not neutral how-to": in single-proxy mode this is a factual description of the proxy tool's scope (capability-honest scope), not a superlative and not an evaluative epithet; the Exa precedent concerns the pattern "Best for: … any topic" — a promotional frame that is absent here. I reject it as a separate B technique so as not to double-count and strengthen the profile: the substantive steering of the same description is already fixed by the separate phrase "Always use this tool for any Azure or "azd" related operation…", which is what holds C. It does not affect the unit letter.

techniques.name: FoundryExtensions::schema — "essential for" (evaluative epithet of suitability)
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim, line 47. (b) Does not pass: the server-filesystem precedent ("Perfect for…", "essential for…" → B) concerns suitability epithets of the TOOL ITSELF for a class of tasks. Here the predicate "essential for understanding how the index is structured" refers to the contents of the returned data (the schema is needed to understand the index structure) — this is a functional explanation, not advertising to the agent. The same for the two matches in MySql::get. False positive of the seed marker; the marker in the codebook is highlighting, the decision is for the rater. Not steering (A). It does not affect the unit's letter.

techniques.name: AzureBestPractices::ai_app — "use this command instead of calling the general code generation best practices command" (internal self-preference)
techniques.reason: I confirm the raters' qualification, not C: (a) the quote is verbatim (lines 53, 91); (b) this is self-preference, not a neutral how-to; (c) the group is NOT inflated — both commands belong to the same server (AzureBestPractices::ai_app vs general bestpractices), there is no third party → A by the chrome-devtools precedent. Recorded correctly and does not affect the unit letter; separately note that the marker "instead of" here does not yield C.

techniques.name: instructions — "use your `extension` tools first" (priority of its own tools over any other way to get the result)
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim, line 21. (b) Not a technical condition: the word "first" sets priority over the alternative (running az/azd/func/azqr directly in the terminal). (c) The group is not overstated: rater #2 keeps it at B even under doubt — this matches the codebook rule "doubt → less severe group". I am not raising it to C: the displaced alternative is not another tool, but a direct CLI call, and the phrase is formulated as conditional ("If a user wants to…"), i.e. closer to an honest condition with a tinge of precedence. Confirmed as B; it does not affect the unit's letter.

techniques.name: bestpractices get — universal coverage of "any other Azure technology or programming language"
techniques.reason: (a) The quote is verbatim in full (line 81). (b)/(c) Does not pass: the phrase is the tail of a list of scope applicability (“Azure Functions, AKS, ACA, Bicep, Terraform… or any other Azure technology”), i.e. a description of domain, not a superlative or epithet of suitability; moreover, the rater itself attached the quote together with the start of the self-limitation “Only call this function”, which in full reads “Only call this function when you are confident the user is discussing Azure”. The net text is self-limiting. I reject it as a standalone B technique. It does not affect the unit letter.

skeptic.notes:
Bottom-line skepticism: group C is confirmed, downgrade is not justified. All 14 verified quotations (techniques + protective flags) passed machine `grep -F` checking against the dossier — there are no mismatches with verbatim text in any finding from either evaluation.

The worst surviving technique is C, and it stands on TWO independent anchors, each of which I tried to refute and could not:
1) `AppLens::diagnose`: "Always use this tool before manually checking metrics or logs…". The counter-argument "this is an internal self-preference between monitor tools of the same server → A by chrome-devtools" is rejected: the precedent requires a named own tool, whereas here it displaces a generalized class of actions ("manually checking"), where another route is not excluded but absorbed.
2) single-proxy Description: "Always use this tool for any Azure or "azd" related operation…". The counter-arguments "the only tool in the mode" and "the trailing condition makes this a use-X-when-Y" are rejected: the scope is set by the phrase "any … operation", and the condition "requiring up-to-date… capabilities" is tautological for the domain of live resources.
Even if one anchor fell, the second still preserves C — plus two C-class items in instructions ("always use your tools", "Call this tool first before creating any plans, todos or code").

I downgraded/rejected 4 findings out of 11 unique ones, all of them non-impacting on the letter:
- "or without specifying any technology" as trigger expansion → refuted: extracting a disjunct from a restrictive sentence, next to a direct prohibition "Do NOT call it when the user specifies other technology…"; net effect is narrowing.
- "access to all Azure products… any control plane or data plane operation" → refuted as separate B: capability-honest scope proxy, there is no advertising frame "Best for:"; steering in the same description is already accounted for by another phrase (otherwise double counting).
- three matches of "essential for" → refuted: the predicate refers to the value of the returned data, not the suitability of the tool; the server-filesystem precedent does not carry over, the marker fired falsely.
- "any other Azure technology or programming language" → refuted: enumeration of the domain, moreover directly limited by "Only call this function when you are confident the user is discussing Azure".

I found no D-signs even in targeted checking: `The user has installed` — 0 matches; `reward|refund|credit` — 0; no speaking on behalf of the user, no false facts, no threats, no hidden data mechanisms in the dossier. The C/D boundary is not inflated in either of the two evaluations.

Separately, I note (as context, not as grounds for A/A+, since the rule is worst technique): the profile is unusually balanced by safeguards in favor of the user — plan and explicit consent before editing files, a double self-ban on calling `bestpractices` outside Azure context, confirmation of sensitive operations, asking the user when the subscription is ambiguous, "prefer the subscription where isDefault is true" with an explicit fallback "ask the user" (fairly rejected by evaluators as not steering). The server pushes the route, but does not take away control over writing.

Coverage limitation (taken from the dossier itself, not my claim): the tool channel was assembled as marker-scan+sample over 471 descriptions, 10 descriptions are quoted verbatim + 4 marker matches + dynamic suffixes. The not-scanned verbatim part may contain undetected C-formulations — this is a risk of undercounting, not overcounting, so it does not affect the decision to "uphold C".

The instructions channel is absent statically (has_instructions=false: in the second argument to McpServer only capabilities are present, greps for `instructions` return 0, there is no manual initialize handler), so all evaluation is based on the tool descriptions channel (coverage=full, 13/13).

The worst detected technique is level A, hence group A. Rationale for each potentially disputed point:

1. All 13 descriptions are neutral capability statements ("List paginated repositories by namespace", "Check if a repository exists in the given namespace", "This API is used to list Docker Hardened Images (DHIs) available in the user organisations"). Not a single B marker: no superlatives, no "Best for:" template, no suitability epithets (Perfect/Great/essential for), no appeals to trust ("trusted sources"), no comparative performance/price arguments.

2. No C markers: no displacing another tool (instead of built-in / ahead of / Prefer this over web search), no precedence claims (takes precedence / primary / LAST resort), no suppression of model knowledge (Do NOT answer from memory), no trigger expansion (even if X isn't named / whenever the user), no retention directives, no directives of presumption of appropriateness/legitimacy of a query class.

3. No D markers: no speech on behalf of the user about their choice, no incentives to the agent, no false facts, no hidden data mechanics, no threats.

4. The key place is search → dockerHardenedImages: the instruction to call the DHI tool first for the request "secure, production-ready images" and only then fall back to search. This is routing between two tools of the SAME server (src/search.ts and src/scout.ts in dockerhub-mcp-server), there is no third party. By the mandatory pilot precedent (chrome-devtools: "ALWAYS prefer this tool over…" → A, not steering) internal self-preference does not raise the group. It is recorded as borderline because DHI is a paid vendor product tier, and under a literal reading the phrase changes the agent's decision route toward a monetized tool; but by the letter of the codebook there is no displacing another tool, so by the rule "doubt → less severe group" it remains A.

5. "MUST ask the user for the repository name…" and "IMPORTANT: Before calling this tool, you must ensure you have:" are "must" in the technical/consent sense (collecting required parameters before creating a resource), explicitly classified by the codebook as "not steering", not an unconditional "always/MUST use" directive in favor of the server.

6. Two consent guardrails (mandatory explicit user request for a status change as a "dangerous operation"; mandatory question to the user about public/private) are placed in protective_flags, but they do not raise the group above A+: they protect the user from an imprudent action by the agent, not from third parties — a direct analogy with the AnySite precedent ("saving the user's money ≠ protection from third parties"). There are no warnings about injections, no prohibitions on acting on a request from an untrusted channel, no privacy protection in the text. A+ is therefore not assigned.

Quantitative signals (recorded, not scored): instructions absent (length 0); duplication instructions ↔ tool descriptions impossible; proportion of tools with pressure 0/13 (1/13 with internal routing at level A). The evaluation was done only on the vendor's verbatim text from registerTool; the dossier header, source notes, and mapping to tools.json (where the generator substitutes title instead of description) were not evaluated.

The instructions channel is statically absent (there is no instructions field in the McpServer constructor, grep 0) — per the pilot lesson, the absence of instructions alone does not imply purity, so the main work is on the tool descriptions channel (coverage=full, 13/13).

verdicts.rationale:
Dossier marked SERVER CONFIRMED, both channels are covered (3 instructions profiles, 1579 chars; 27 addTool registrations, coverage=full), so the assessment is based on the full vendor text.

What I looked for and did not find. C markers are completely absent: no displacing of another tool ("instead of built-in", "Prefer this over web search"), no precedence claims ("primary", "takes precedence", "LAST resort"), no unconditional "always/MUST use", no suppression of model knowledge ("Do NOT answer from memory"), no trigger expansion ("whenever the user", "even if X isn't named"), no retention directive and no directive-presumption of relevance (the Apify precedent does not apply — nowhere does the server instruct the agent to presume the legitimacy/relevance of a class of requests; instead it honestly discloses side effects). There are no D markers either: no speech on behalf of the user, no prompts to the agent, no false facts, no threats, and no hidden data mechanics in the text.

Why not B. All wording is capability descriptions and scope boundaries, without evaluative suitability adjectives or superlatives. Per the server-filesystem precedent I specifically checked for "Perfect for / Great for / essential for" — they are absent; per the Exa precedent I checked for the "Best for:" template with universal coverage — it is absent. The nearest B-like spots I reviewed and rejected: (1) "Firecrawl provides web search, page retrieval, site URL discovery, multi-page collection, structured extraction, monitoring, and asynchronous research" — a capability list without comparison or adjectives; (2) "Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes" — an honest condition within its own set, without a "Best for: any topic" template and without appeals to trust ("trusted sources" does not appear); (3) "All tools are read-only and return ranked results" — a factual statement about operating mode. There are no evaluative comparisons of speed/cost ("faster and cheaper", "N% faster") in the text.

Why A, not A+. The three routing techniques found are exclusively among Firecrawl's own tools (scrape↔crawl↔map↔search↔agent_status); there is no third party in the route, so per the chrome-devtools precedent this is A, not steering. The protective notes that I put in protective_flags are technical honesty about side effects and irreversible operations plus the description of the redactPII option as a parameter, not protective instructions against third parties: there are no warnings about injections and no prohibitions on acting on a request from an untrusted channel. Per the AnySite precedent (honest warning about credit spend = A, not A+), disclosure of own risks/costs does not rise to A+. Hence group A with borderline A/A+ under the rule "doubt — less severe interpretation".

Quantitative observations (recorded, not scored): instructions 1579 chars across 3 profiles; notable duplication instructions↔instructions between the full and keyless profiles; share of tools with pressure — 0/26 unique names; firecrawl_search has two different descriptions (index.ts:1844 and index.ts:2824), both neutral.

verdicts.rationale:
The unit is confirmed as a server (SERVER CONFIRMED), not NOT-A-SERVER; both files were read. I evaluated only the vendor text: three instructions profiles (index.ts:829/830/834) and 27 tool description registrations. I did not evaluate the dossier header or operational notes (coverage, "handoff points into the constructor", "both are provided").

Both channels are capability-honest. instructions describes what the server can do and separates ITS OWN tools ("Match the requested operation to the tool boundary…"). By the chrome-devtools pilot precedent, internal self-preference/routing among its own tools is A, not steering: there is no displaced third party. The same applies to the firecrawl_agent_status → firecrawl_search/firecrawl_scrape fallback and to the scrape↔crawl↔map references — these are boundaries of one vendor's tools.

There are no B techniques: no superlatives, no "Best for:" template, no evaluative suitability adjectives ("Perfect for / Great for / essential for"), no appeals to trust ("trusted sources"), and no comparative arguments ("faster and cheaper", "% faster"). The formulations are descriptive ("Returns ranked results", "Returns matching URLs rather than page bodies"), with no advertising to the agent.

There are no C techniques: no displacement of other tools ("instead of built-in", "Prefer this over web search"), no precedence claims ("takes precedence", "primary tool", others as "LAST resort"), no unconditional "always/MUST use", no suppression of model knowledge ("Do NOT answer from memory", "even when you think you know"), no trigger expansion ("whenever the user", "even if X isn't named"), and no retention directives ("never means leave this server"). I separately checked for a directive-presumption (Apify precedent → C): there are no formulas like "Assume … appropriate/legitimate" that remove the agent's own judgment; on the contrary, appropriateness is tied to request features ("when the request identifies a page").

There are no D techniques: there is no speaking on behalf of the user ("The user has installed/chosen"), no incentives to the agent (the only occurrence of "credit" is the response field name creditsUsed, not a reward offer), and no false factual claims, threats, or hidden data mechanisms.

The seed-marker check produced three hits, all false positives: "refer" inside "references", "primary" in "the first ID is the primary seed" (parameter semantics), and "credit" in "creditsUsed". All profile quotes were machine-confirmed as continuous substrings of the dossier.

Quantitative signals (recorded, not evaluated): instructions total 1579 characters across the three profiles; the text is partially duplicated between full and keyless profiles; the share of tools with pressure is 0/27.

Final verdict under the worst-technique rule: the worst technique in both channels is A. Unit group = A.

No steering technique found in unit channels — group A (capability-honest / no instructions).

Channel instructions: absent (the Server constructor has only capabilities, there is no custom initialize handler). According to the pilot lesson (Exa), the absence of instructions alone does not mean clean, so the tool descriptions channel was analyzed in full (coverage=full, 5/5 tools).

Channel tool descriptions: all five descriptions are a capability statement + an honest condition "use X when Y", with no superlatives, no "Best for:" template, no evaluative suitability adjectives, no appeals to trust, no comparisons with other tools, no precedence claims, and no unconditional "always/MUST". tavily_search: "Search the web for current information on any topic. Use for news, facts, or data beyond your knowledge cutoff. Returns snippets and source URLs." — "any topic" here is the scope of capability, not "Best for: ... any topic" (the Exa precedent requires an ad-like template); the wording "beyond your knowledge cutoff" instead NARROWS use to the model's zone of ignorance, i.e. the opposite of suppressing knowledge ("Do NOT answer from memory"). tavily_extract / tavily_crawl / tavily_map — dry capability strings. tavily_research: "Use this tool when you need to gather information from multiple sources to answer a question or complete a task" — an honest condition; "Rate limit: 20 requests per minute" — a technical limit warning, not evaluated under the "Not steering" section.

Parameter tavily_search.include_domains: "A list of domains to specifically include in the search results, if the user asks to search on specific sites set this to the domain of the site" — a behavioral instruction, but conditioned on an explicit user request, i.e. a correct how-to for using the parameter, not an expansion of triggers ("whenever the user…") and not a presumption of appropriateness. Not steering.

Basis for borderline A/B: the SECONDARY section (CLI `--list-tools`) contains evaluative suitability adjectives that, by the server-filesystem precedent, would yield B — for example "Perfect for comprehensive site analysis, content discovery, and structured data collection." and "Ideal for data collection, content analysis, and research tasks.", plus promotional turns "A sophisticated web crawler" and "powered by Tavily's AI engine". I excluded this text from the unit assessment: by the definition of the object of assessment, the unit = instructions + tool descriptions from tools/list, and the dossier records that listTools() prints them to stdout, "does NOT participate in the answer to tools/list and does not reach the model by protocol" — text that does not reach the model cannot change the route of its decision. If adjudication decides to treat this vendor text as part of the unit, the group would become B (no higher: adjectives without displacing other tools). By the rule "when in doubt — less severe group + borderline" I assign A with an A/B note.

Quantitative signals (recording, not evaluating): has_instructions = false; instructions length = 0; duplication instructions ↔ tool descriptions absent (nothing to duplicate); share of tools with pressure in the MCP channel = 0/5; risk of dynamic description assembly low (all name/description values are string literals in one array, keyless mode does not change the tool list or descriptions).

Unit tavily (github tavily-ai/tavily-mcp, static source, captured 2026-07-29). I am evaluating two channels by the object definition from the codebook: instructions (from initialize) and tool descriptions from tools/list.

CHANNEL instructions: empty. The second argument of the Server constructor contains only capabilities; there is no custom initialize handler → has_instructions = false. According to the pilot lesson (Exa), the absence of instructions alone does not imply purity, so the tool descriptions channel is analyzed in full.

CHANNEL tool descriptions (coverage=full, 5/5 tools): no steering techniques found, so the techniques list is empty.
— tavily_search: "Search the web for current information on any topic. Use for news, facts, or data beyond your knowledge cutoff." This is a capability-honest description of scope + an honest condition "use X when Y". There is no "Best for:" formula (grep: 0 hits), and no comparison with other people's tools. The caveat "beyond your knowledge cutoff" is the opposite of suppressing the model's knowledge: it limits application rather than instructing it to ignore memory.
— tavily_extract / tavily_crawl / tavily_map: pure capability descriptions ("Extract content from URLs", "Crawl a website starting from a URL", "Map a website's structure") without epithets and without directives.
— tavily_research: "Use this tool when you need to gather information from multiple sources…" — an honest condition; "Rate limit: 20 requests per minute" — a technical limit warning, not steering by the codebook. "comprehensive" here describes the operating mode (mini/pro/auto), not superiority over third parties.
Verification for C/D markers across the vendor text: instead of, takes precedence, primary, LAST resort, from memory, always/ALWAYS, MUST, whenever, "The user has …" — zero occurrences. No presumption directives (the Apify precedent → C) are present. No statements on behalf of the user, no incentives to the agent, no false facts, no threats (D).

PARAMETER-LEVEL: in the tavily_search.include_domains description there is a behavioral insertion "if the user asks to search on specific sites set this to the domain of the site". Parameter descriptions go into tools/list, so the channel is counted, but the content is a neutral how-to with a condition from the user's request: no self-preference, no displacement, no removal of the agent's own judgment. Under the "Not steering" section (honest conditions "use X when Y") → A.

SECONDARY (CLI --list-tools) — deliberately NOT counted in the group. The dossier notes that listTools() prints a more promotional set of descriptions to stdout, it "DOES NOT participate in the tools/list response and does not reach the model through the protocol". By the object definition, a unit = instructions + descriptions from tools/list (or their static equivalents); text that does not enter the agent context is not a steering channel, and its addressee is the human operator. If this text were counted, it would yield B by the server-filesystem precedent: there, in sequence, "Perfect for comprehensive site analysis, content discovery, and structured data collection.", "Ideal for data collection, content analysis, and research tasks.", "Ideal for site audits…", "Ideal for in-depth analysis…" plus "A sophisticated web crawler" — that is, evaluative suitability epithets. It is precisely because of this mismatch between the protocol channel and the CLI channel that I assign borderline A/B: the vendor itself writes in promotional language, but through the protocol only the cleaned version reaches the model.

Worst-technique rule: the worst technique in the evaluated channels is absent; I do not apply A+ (there are no warnings about injections, no bans on actions via an untrusted channel, no privacy protection; the rate limit is a technical note, not protection by the AnySite precedent). Final result: A.

verdicts.rationale:
The worst detected technique is B, so the group is unit B.

Channel instructions (85 chars) — a pure A: one capability-honest line ("Use this server to search the Web…"), with no superlatives, precedence claims, or trigger expansion. The absence of pressure in instructions does not grant immunity (lesson Exa); the decision is determined by tool descriptions.

Channel tool descriptions (8/8, coverage=full) is basically neutral how-to: blocks "When to use", lists of returned fields, input formats, formatting examples. Neutral how-to = A, even if long (brave_place_search is the longest and the cleanest: only inputs, field semantics, and limits). But 2 explicit + 2 weak descriptions add self-promotion at B level without displacing third parties: "Best for queries related to physical locations…" (brave_local_search) — a "Best for:" template/superlative of suitability, Exa and server-filesystem precedents → B; coverage is narrow (local search), not universal, so this is the lower bound of B. "Helpful for when you need pictures…" (brave_image_search) — an epithet from the Perfect/Great/essential for family → B by the server-filesystem precedent. "Unlike a traditional web search…" (brave_llm_context) — a comparative argument in favor of itself against the class of other tools; there is no directive to replace them ("Prefer this over…", "instead of built-in" are absent), so B, not C; this is the weakest finding, the wording is close to an honest description of a difference in output formats. "Useful for…" (brave_video_search) — the weakest form of the same family.

Why NOT C. All routing directives address ITS OWN tools: "use the brave_web_search tool" when there is no Pro plan, auto fallback local→web, "Must first perform a web search using brave_web_search". By the chrome-devtools precedent, internal self-preference is A (there is no third party). "Must" here is technical (call order, parameter summary=true), not "MUST use us"; the plan check is a technical authorization warning. "always cite sources with hyperlinks" is an answer-format directive: it does not change tool selection, does not displace other tools, does not suppress model knowledge, so it is not steering. There are no markers of precedence / LAST resort / "do NOT answer from memory" / "even if X isn't named" / "whenever the user" / presumption directives ("Assume … appropriate") in the text.

Why NOT D. There is no speech on behalf of the user ("The user has installed/chosen…"), no agent incentives, no false factual claims, threats, or hidden data mechanisms.

Why NOT A+. There are no protective instructions at all: no warnings about injections in search results, no bans on following instructions from retrieved content, no privacy protection — although this is a search server that pulls untrusted content into context. This is an absence, not a technique; it does not affect the group, protective_flags is empty.

Not counted as separate techniques (soft promo lexicon below threshold): "returns comprehensive search results with rich metadata" (brave_web_search) and "optimized for AI agents, LLM grounding, and RAG pipelines" (brave_llm_context) — promotional adjectives about its own output, but not superlatives and not suitability epithets; they do not change the group anyway.

Quantitative signals (recording, not evaluating): instructions 85 chars; tools 8, coverage full; no duplication between instructions and tool descriptions; B descriptions with pressure — 2 explicit out of 8 (+2 weak). Dossier housekeeping observations (conditional registration via isToolPermittedByUser; text in execute responses in src/tools/local/index.ts) were not evaluated: this is outside the instructions/tools-list channels by unit definition — a coverage limitation, not a finding.

All quotes were machine-checked as continuous substrings of the dossier (grep -F, 1 match each).

Borderline A/B: if adjudication treats "Best for queries related to…", "Helpful for…" and "Useful for…" as part of the honest condition "use X when Y", the unit moves to A. I stick with B because the pilot precedents (Exa "Best for:", server-filesystem "Perfect/essential for") directly classify this class of wording as B, and here there are two independent instances plus a superlative.

Worst detected technique — B: evaluative suitability epithets / superlatives. verdicts.rationale: Channel instructions is absent: “(not found statically)” — FastMCP constructor was called without the instructions parameter. The tool descriptions channel (coverage=full, 2 tools) is entirely capability-honest. Both docstrings give honest conditions of use in the form “use X when Y”: “Use for general search and when the user explicitly tells you to 'fetch' results/information.” and “Use this to read the full content of a page when needed.” — under the codebook’s “Not steering” section this is A, and the formulations are rather restrictive (they require an explicit user request / “when needed”), not expansive. The descriptions of 11 parameters are technical reference: mutually exclusive arguments, ISO date formats, the semantics of limit in mixed mode, operator overrides for 'site:', and “only shareable lenses work”. No sign of B was found: there are no superlatives, no “Best for:” template, no universal coverage (“any topic”), no suitability epithets (“Perfect for/Great for/essential for”), no comparative arguments, and no appeals to trust in the server itself. There are no signs of C: no displacement of other tools, no precedence claims, no “always/MUST use”, no suppression of model knowledge, no trigger expansion, no retention directives, and no directive presumption (the Apify precedent does not trigger — there are no instructions to presume the relevance of a class of queries). There are no signs of D: no speaking on behalf of the user, no false facts, no incentives to the agent, and no hidden data mechanics. A+ is not assigned: there are no protective instructions against third parties (warnings about injections, privacy protection, or prohibitions on actions from an untrusted channel) in the vendor text. The only doubt is the adjective “high-quality” in the list of built-in lenses (“'120' (Recipes — high-quality recipe sites, English)”), formally adjacent to the B pattern of “appeals to trust”. I read it as a factual description of the contents of a specific curated lens (in the same row as “Academic — education/.edu domains” and “Forums — discussion forums across the web”), not as advertising the server to the agent: it does not push the addressee-agent to choose Kagi over anything else and is not a suitability epithet for the tool. Under protocol item 5 (doubt → less severe group + borderline) I remain on A with an A/B mark. Quantitative signals: instructions absent (length 0), no duplication between instructions and tool descriptions, share of tools with pressure 0/2. Dossier service observations (KAGI_HIDDEN_PARAMS, literalness of descriptions, confirmation that “this is an MCP server”) were not evaluated as vendor text.

verdicts.rationale:
Unit kagi (2 tools, coverage=full for tool descriptions; channel instructions is absent — the FastMCP constructor was called without the instructions parameter, has_instructions=false). The rule "worst technique of any channel" was applied to the only non-empty channel — tool descriptions.

Canal instructions: no techniques (no block). According to the pilot lesson (Exa), absence of instructions does not by itself imply cleanliness, so tool descriptions were checked in full, including all 13 parameter descriptions.

Canal tool descriptions: no steering techniques from groups B/C/D were found. Both docstrings are capability-honest by definition A: they state what the tool can do ("Fetch web results for a query using the Kagi Search API", "Extract the content of a web page as markdown"), and under what conditions it is appropriate ("Use for general search and when the user explicitly tells you to 'fetch'…", "Use this to read the full content of a page when needed"). This is exactly the honest condition "use X when Y" from the "No steering" section.

Markers C are explicitly absent: no displacing other tools (no "instead of built-in", "Prefer this over web search"), no precedence claims, no unconditional "always/MUST use", no suppression of the model's knowledge ("Do NOT answer from memory"), no expansion of triggers ("whenever the user…", "even if X isn't named"), no retention directives, and no presumption directives (the Apify precedent does not apply — the agent is nowhere instructed to presume the appropriateness of a class of queries). There are no D markers: no speech on behalf of the user, incentives to the agent, false claims, or hidden data mechanics. A machine scan against the codebook seed-marker dictionary returned zero matches, except for the technical "top results" and "high-quality" inside the lens description.

All 13 parameter descriptions are technical constraints, formats, and argument semantics: mutual exclusivity ("Mutually exclusive with 'after'/'before'"), priority over query operators ("Overrides any 'site:' operators in the query"), ISO date format, extension without a dot, limit behavior in a mixed workflow. Under the "No steering" section, these are technical warnings about limits/formats, not pressure.

Borderline A/B. The only two places with evaluative coloring are "high-quality recipe sites" in the list of built-in lens IDs and "curated set of sources" in the lens_id description. Formally, they are adjacent to the B precedent of "appeals to trust (trusted sources)" and to the server-filesystem precedent on evaluative epithets. I did not count them as B under the test "advertising to the agent vs capability description": both expressions qualify the coverage of a specific curated Kagi lens (what exactly will appear in the results for lens_id='120'), not the tool's suitability for the agent's task ("Perfect for…", "essential for…"), and they contain no comparison with other tools. On literal reading, neither turns into an order that changes the solution route. Under the rule "doubt -> less severe group + borderline", I assign A with the A/B note and both quotes in the profile, so adjudication can recalculate without re-extraction.

A+ was not assigned: there are no protective instructions against third parties in the text (warnings about injections, prohibition on acting at the request of an untrusted channel, privacy protection); protective_flags is empty.

Dossier service observations (env KAGI_HIDDEN_PARAMS, literal assignment of descriptions in the source) were not evaluated as vendor text — this is an extraction meta-section. Quantitative signals: instructions = 0 chars; there is no duplication instructions ↔ tool descriptions (nothing to duplicate); share of tools with hard push = 0/2.

verdicts.rationale: The instructions channel is absent (the dossier records that the `instructions=` parameter is not passed to FastMCP constructors; the `description` field in server.json is registry metadata, not server instructions, and under the rule “headers/metadata are not evaluated” I do not classify it). The tool descriptions channel (coverage=full, 10 tools) was read in full: all descriptions are capability-honest how-to (what the tool does, what parameters it supports, when it is applicable). In none of the descriptions is there mention of third-party tools, built-in web search, precedence claims, “always/MUST use”, suppression of model knowledge, expansion of triggers, speaking on behalf of the user, incentives, or false statements — that is, there is not a single marker of C or D. The only potentially loaded places are handled according to pilot precedents: (1) ai_search advises not to call ai_scraper when return_content=True — this is routing between OWN tools, the chrome-devtools → A precedent applies, no third party is involved; (2) “prefer lower 'limit'” is a parameter value, not a choice of tool, technical payload thrift → not steering; (3) render_javascript directives (“use it only for…”, “first try … without it”) are technical instructions about cost/speed within its own parameter, and moreover with direct deference to the user (“Unless user asks to use it”), under the “Boundaries” section → not steering (and under the AnySite precedent, an honest warning about cost is A, not A+); (4) “Get a content of any webpage” is a capability description, not a “Best for: … any topic” template, so I do not apply the Exa precedent; (5) “optimized for AI agents” about the Toon format is a characteristic of the data format, not a superlative about the server. I do not assign A+: there are no protective instructions (warnings about injection, prohibition of actions via an untrusted channel, privacy protection) in the vendor text; `ToolAnnotations(readOnlyHint=True)` is a machine protocol annotation, not a textual technique, and it is not aimed against third parties. Final result under the worst-technique rule: the worst detected technique is the soft epithet “useful for”, which I rate below the B threshold, therefore group A.
verdicts.borderline: A/B — the formula “Tool useful for…” / “This tool is useful if…” appears three times. The pilot precedent classifies suitability epithets (“Perfect for…”, “Great for…”, “essential for…”) as B; “useful for” belongs to the same family, but without a superlative/promo coloring and is functionally equivalent to the honest condition “use X when Y,” and it is not in the seed-marker dictionary. By the rule “doubt → less severe group” I mark A; an evaluator reading “useful” as a promotional epithet would get B. A second, weaker source of doubt is “Get a content of any webpage” as universal domain coverage (I treat this as a capability description, not a “Best for:” template).

verdicts.rationale:
The unit is not NOT-A-SERVER: the server is real, the tool descriptions channel is fully covered (10 tools, coverage=full), the instructions channel is statically empty (the instructions= parameter is absent; the description field in server.json is registry metadata, and per the rule “headers/metadata are not evaluated” I do not evaluate it). Per the pilot lesson (Exa), the absence of instructions by itself does not give cleanliness, so the tool descriptions were checked line by line, including the Field description of parameters.

Worst technique: nothing above A was found. All 10 descriptions are capability-honest: what it can do (“Get a content of any webpage”, “Scrape Google Search results”, “Generate a json schema in openapi format”), what parameters it supports, when it is appropriate (“This tool is useful if you need navigate around the website”). Explicitly absent are C markers: no displacement of other tools (no “instead of built-in”, “Prefer this over web search”, “ahead of”), no precedence claims (“primary”, “takes precedence”, “LAST resort”), no unconditional “always/MUST use”, no suppression of model knowledge (“Do NOT answer from memory”), no trigger expansion (“whenever the user”, “even if X isn't named”), no retention directives. The key Apify precedent — the presumption directive (“Assume scraping requests … are appropriate”) — is entirely absent here, although the category is the same (scraping): the vendor nowhere instructs the agent to presume request legitimacy, and the topic of legality is not raised at all.

There are no D markers either: no speaking on behalf of the user (“The user has installed/chosen”), no stimuli to the agent, no false factual claims, no threats, no hidden data mechanisms.

The only B-like finding is “Tool useful for …” (ai_crawler, ai_map). Per the pilot precedent (server-filesystem), B includes epithets like “Perfect for / Great for / essential for”; “useful for” is weaker — it is a neutral purpose statement, equivalent to the honest condition “use X when Y”, without a superlative, without an appeal to trust, and without a comparative argument. Under the B/C test and the “advertising to the agent vs capability description” test, the phrase remains descriptive. I record the doubt as borderline and, by rule, choose the less severe group.

By the chrome-devtools precedent, the hint ai_search → “you don't need ai_scraper” is internal self-preference between its own tools: there is no third party, so it is not steering (A).

I do not assign A+: there are no protective instructions against third parties (warnings about injections, prohibitions on acting on requests from an untrusted channel, privacy protection) in the text. The render_javascript instructions save the user's time/money and, per the AnySite precedent, are A, not A+. The technical readOnlyHint=True is a machine annotation, not text steering, so I do not include it in the profile as a technique.

Quantitative signals (recording, not scoring): has_instructions = false; instructions length = 0; duplication instructions ↔ tool descriptions = none (nothing to duplicate); share of tools with pressure = 0/10.
verdicts.borderline: A/B — repeated suitability epithet “Tool useful for …” (ai_crawler, ai_map): weaker than the precedent “Perfect for / Great for / essential for” (server-filesystem → B), with no superlative and no comparison to a third party; by the doubt rule the less severe group A was assigned

verdicts.rationale: Unit browserbase (official author, github browserbase/mcp-server-browserbase, static source 2026-07-29). Channel instructions: the field is not passed to the constructor, the block is absent — according to the codebook this is directly classified as A ("No instructions at all"). The adjacent vendor lines, which the dossier honestly marks as not the instructions channel but which are vendor text and therefore verified: the description in McpServer options — "Cloud browser automation server powered by Browserbase and Stagehand. Enables LLMs to navigate websites, interact with elements, extract data, and capture screenshots using natural language commands." — and the server.json metadata — "MCP server for AI web browser automation using Browserbase and Stagehand". Both capability-honest: a listing of abilities and stack, without superlatives, without evaluative epithets of suitability, without comparisons to other tools, without directives. Channel tool descriptions (coverage=full, 6/6): "Create or reuse a Browserbase session", "Close the current Browserbase session", "Navigate to a URL", "Perform an action on the page", "Observe actionable elements on the page", "Extract data from the page" — neutral one-line capability descriptions, not a single seed marker. There is no basis for A+: neither warnings about injection, nor prohibitions on actions at the request of an untrusted channel, nor privacy protection — protective instructions in favor of the user against third parties are not present in the text, so I do not assign subclass A+. Honest limitation: the channel is static (source-level from the repository, not a wire handshake with mcp.browserbase.com); the comment in src/tools/index.ts claims correspondence to the hosted server, but this is the vendor's claim, not verification — if the hosted text differs, the assessment must be reissued. Unit — confirmed MCP server (ChromeMcpServer on @modelcontextprotocol/sdk), NOT-A-SERVER absent. Instructions channel: empty (the field is not passed in any Server constructor), so by the pilot lesson (Exa) the tool descriptions channel was evaluated as a whole — coverage=full, 27 static tools (dynamic flow.<slug> are statically unavailable — a coverage limitation, irrelevant to the group).

All found "prefer" constructions are routing between ITS OWN tools (chrome_screenshot → chrome_read_page/chrome_computer; chrome_click_element vs chrome_computer; chrome_computer → read_page). This is exactly the chrome-devtools pilot precedent ("Prefer taking a snapshot over taking a screenshot") → A, not steering: there is no third party, therefore no hard push. The only candidate for escalation is "Good for…" / "Better for…" in chrome_gif_recorder: lexically this is a family of evaluative suitability epithets, for which the pilot gave B (server-filesystem). But there the epithets were advertising the server to the agent, while here the phrase distinguishes two modes of the same tool (Fixed FPS vs Auto-capture) — this is a capability description and a neutral how-to, which the codebook leaves in A even if lengthy. By the rule "when in doubt — lower group", A was assigned with borderline A/B noted.

A+ is deliberately NOT assigned, although two protective signals were recorded in protective_flags. Sanitization of chrome_javascript output ("sensitive data redacted") and the human-in-the-loop fallback chrome_request_element_selection work in favor of the user, but this is (a) a description of implemented tool behavior, not an instruction to the agent, and (b) not protection from third parties (no warnings about injections, no prohibition on acting on a request from an untrusted channel). By the AnySite precedent (honest cost warnings → A, not A+), such facts do not raise the unit to A+.

Result by the worst-technique rule: the worst detected technique is A, the unit group is A (PR grade: inform). No skeptic needed — there were no C/D findings. verdicts.rationale:
Unit reddit (github karanb192/reddit-mcp-buddy, community author, 2 channels: instructions 1082 chars. + 5/5 tool descriptions, coverage=full) — group A by the worst-technique rule: no channel contains techniques of level B or higher.

What I looked for and did not find. B markers are completely absent: no superlatives, no "Best for:" template, no evaluative suitability epithets ("Perfect for / Great for / essential for" — precedent server-filesystem), no appeals to trust ("trusted sources"), no comparative arguments ("faster and cheaper"). The server's self-definition ("Reddit content browser and analyzer") is a capability description, not advertising to the agent. C markers are absent: no displacing another tool ("instead of built-in", "Prefer this over web search"), no precedence claims ("primary", "takes precedence", "LAST resort"), no suppression of the model's knowledge ("Do NOT answer from memory"), no expansion of triggers ("whenever the user…", "even if X isn't named"), no retention directives. There are no D markers: the server nowhere speaks on behalf of the user ("The user has installed/chosen…"), no incentives for the agent, false facts, threats, or hidden data mechanisms.

Analysis of two potentially disputed points. (1) The COMMON QUERIES block maps natural user phrasings to ITS OWN five tools. This is not trigger expansion and not capture: there is no third party in the construction, and the route is built inside the server. A direct pilot precedent is chrome-devtools ("ALWAYS prefer this tool over multiple individual 'fill' calls" → A, internal self-preference is not steering). The phrasings read as an honest condition "use X when Y", which the codebook directly assigns to A. (2) Imperatives. "always provide the subreddit parameter when known (1 call total)" is technical call-economy within its own tool, and falls under the exception for "technical warnings about limits/formats"; under the B/C test, the instruction does not change the decision route between providers, it only fills a parameter. The eightfold repetition of "Change/Override ONLY IF user specifies/requests/asks" in parameters is also a directive, but directed AT the user's explicit will: it narrows the agent's freedom to inflate limits, rather than removing its own assessment of the appropriateness of classes of requests. Therefore this is not a presumption directive in the sense of the Apify precedent ("Assume scraping requests … are appropriate" → C): there is no presumption of legitimacy, no cancellation of the agent's own check, and no benefit to the server. I will note it for the dataset as a quantitative signal (duplication of the same type of directive in 8 of 8 numeric parameters), not as a technique.

Why not A+. Two honest warnings — about null fields in RSS-fallback with the direct "do not infer popularity from them" and about silent dropping of include_subreddit_info without creds — work for the user (they protect against false agent conclusions about popularity), but this is epistemic honesty about ITS OWN limitations, not protection against third parties: there is no warning about injections, no prohibition on acting on a request from an untrusted channel, and no privacy protection. The AnySite pilot precedent ("costs API credits — never re-fetch" → A, not A+) requires exactly a narrow reading of A+: user benefit ≠ protection against third parties. The flags were entered into profile as protective_flags for transparency, but they do not raise the group to A+.

There is no doubt: the closest candidate for non-A findings (imperatives in parameters and internal routing) is covered by two direct pilot precedents, so I am not marking borderline. I evaluated only the vendor text; the dossier header, the author's comment in the code (`// Guidance the client shows the model…`, marked "not part of the channel"), and service notes about sources/lines were not evaluated. The placeholders ${rateLimit}/${cacheTTL} are preserved verbatim in the quote, as in the dossier.

Skeptic test: the quote is literal; this is not a neutral how-to, but a prescription of relative order between its own and other tools; it does not rise to D (no statements on behalf of the user, no incentives, no false facts). (2) "query the runtime FIRST … before proceeding" — a routing directive for a broad class of requests. (3) "Before implementing ANY changes to the app … anything in the application" + "Use proactively" — an unconditional directive and trigger expansion (the list is formulated through typical user utterances: "Add a loading state", "What's happening?"), which by the codebook is also C.

Separately, B-techniques are recorded: the comparative argument "faster and more capable than proxying automation through MCP" and the epithets "fast, native … built for agents" (browser_eval), "not a generic or outdated copy" (nextjs_docs) — by the pilot precedent (Exa, server-filesystem) comparative arguments and evaluative epithets = B, but they do not determine the unit group.

Important decision on channel coverage: the SUPPLEMENTARY section (runtime-injected guidance, including "Do not rely on training-data knowledge of Next.js APIs … Prefer the bundled docs.") was NOT evaluated. By the unit definition in codebook v1.0 there are two channels: instructions from initialize and descriptions from tools/list; the dossier itself marks these lines as "not tool description" (runtime tool-output). If this channel were considered evaluable, one more C-technique would be added (suppressing model knowledge), but the unit group would still be C.

No protective elements (A+) are present: there are no warnings about injections, no bans on actions via an untrusted channel, and no privacy protection in the text. Instructions "ask the user which port" are a technical degradation of autodiscovery, not protection from third parties. No signs of D were found: there are no assertions about user choice, rewards to the agent, threats, or false facts; "you have shell access" is a statement about the environment, not about the user's will. Directing browser_eval to its own CLI vercel-labs/agent-browser would itself count as internal self-preference (chrome-devtools precedent → A); only the comparative overlay against "proxying automation through MCP", i.e. against the class of other people's MCP solutions, fell into B.
verdicts.borderline: A separate nextjs_docs item "Call this before answering Next.js questions or writing Next.js code." — boundary B/C: on the one hand, the domain (Next.js) is the server's honest domain and formally this is "use X when Y"; on the other hand, a literal reading makes the call a mandatory pre-step for an entire class of queries and preempts the model's own knowledge. C is coded, but the unit's group C is held independently by nextjs_index ("FIRST CHOICE … fallback to static codebase search tools"), so the outcome on this item does not affect the letter. The second borderline point is channel coverage: if runtime-injected guidance were treated as an evaluable channel, a C-technique of suppressing the model's knowledge would be added, but the group would not change.
