verdicts.rationale: SERVER CONFIRMED, not NOT-A-SERVER. The instructions channel is absent statically (has_instructions=false), so all steering lives in tool descriptions — exactly the pilot lesson from Exa: empty instructions ≠ purity. The worst channel technique tool descriptions = C, hence the unit group C by the worst-technique rule. The core of C is in `nextjs_index`: "Use this as FIRST CHOICE for searching the currently running app. If not found, fallback to static codebase search tools" — this is direct displacement of others' (built-in / host) search tools, demoting them to fallback, the family of "instead of built-in" / others as LAST resort; and "query the runtime FIRST … before proceeding" — a precedence directive. Attached to them are the unconditional premise "Before implementing ANY changes to the app" and the proactivity instruction "Use proactively in these scenarios" with a long list of user phrasings (trigger expansion). The B/C test passes unambiguously: under a literal reading, the phrases change the agent's decision route rather than bragging about capabilities. Important: this is NOT a precedent of internal self-preference (chrome-devtools → A): the fallback static-search tools belong to the host/third parties, not Vercel, so a third party is present. B-layer: the comparative argument "faster and more capable than proxying automation through MCP" and the epithets "a fast, native browser-automation CLI built for agents" promote the own CLI `agent-browser` (the comparison is against the class of MCP proxying, i.e. against other browser servers, but without a directive "use instead of" — therefore B, not C); "not a generic or outdated copy" is a similar soft devaluation of alternative sources. Separately on doubts: "Call this before answering Next.js questions or writing Next.js code" I keep as C (an unconditional directive-premise for the whole domain, a soft form of "do not answer from memory"), but I acknowledge it is borderline B/C; at the unit-group level this does not matter — C is already firmly fixed by the quote about FIRST CHOICE, so I do not assign borderline at the unit level. D not found: there is no speech on behalf of the user ("The user has installed/chosen…"), no incentives to the agent, no hidden data mechanisms, no verifiably false facts (claims about /_next/mcp in Next.js 16+ are technical, outside my verification, but do not present themselves as the user's will). A+ not found: there are no warnings about injections, no bans on acting on requests from an untrusted channel, and no privacy protection. I did not evaluate as techniques: (1) the SUPPLEMENTARY section (`nextjs-docs.ts:113` "Do not rely on training-data knowledge … Prefer the bundled docs", ai_instruction in nextjs_index) — by unit definition this is runtime tool-output, not the instructions channel or a tool description; I note it as an out-of-channel signal which, if placed into a channel, would give the same C (suppression of model knowledge + "Prefer"); (2) the REQUIREMENTS about Next.js 16+ and "upgrade first by running 'npx @next/codemod@latest upgrade latest'" — I treat it as a technical version requirement (per the "Not steering" section), although it is also a directive to change the user's project for the server to work; I record it as an observation, not as a technique; (3) the dossier header and service notes. Quantitative signals: has_instructions=false; 4 tools, of which 3 out of 4 have pressure (browser_eval, nextjs_docs, nextjs_index), the most loaded one is nextjs_index (~45 lines, half of them routing directives); no duplication of instructions ↔ tool descriptions because the first channel is absent.

techniques.name: Displacing other/built-in tools: own as FIRST CHOICE, other as fallback (tool_description:nextjs_index)
techniques.reason: (a) The quote is verbatim and continuous — the grep -F check in the dossier passed in both forms (with the prefix “3. **For agentic codebase search**:” and without). (b) Not neutral how-to and not a technical condition: the phrase does not describe what the tool can do, but sets the order of invocation between tools owned by different parties — “FIRST CHOICE” for its own and “fallback” for “static codebase search tools” owned by the host agent. (c) The group is not overstated: this is exactly the C pattern “instead of built-in” / the other tool as last resort; the chrome-devtools precedent (internal self-preference → A) does not apply, because a third party is present. I tried to refute it in two ways — both failed: (1) “the claim is factually true, static search really does not see runtime” — the codebook gives no exception for the truthfulness of the superiority claim; the B/C test is purely formal (“does the phrase become an order that changes the decision route”), and here it does so literally; (2) “narrow scope — only running app” — narrowing the scope softens it, but the C definition does not contain a threshold for domain width, and downgrading to B is impossible: B is “we are best in X” without a directive, here the directive to downgrade the other tool to fallback is explicit. It does not rise to D (there is no speech on behalf of the user, false facts, incentives, threats) — so it is not overstated upward either.

techniques.name: Precedence directive for routing: "query the runtime FIRST … before proceeding" (tool_description:nextjs_index)
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim, verified with grep -F. (b) Not how-to: "KEY PRINCIPLE" + "FIRST" + "before proceeding" is an order of sequence, not a description of capability or a technical limitation. (c) C is justified: the strongest skeptic objection is "this is an honest condition of the form use X when Y, the condition 'if the request involves the running Next.js application' merely delineates the scope of applicability". I reject that objection: the condition coincides with the tool's full domain, so within the domain the directive is unconditional, and the burden is carried not by the words "if involves" but by "FIRST … before proceeding" — a precedence claim from the definition of C, a functional equivalent of "always call this first". A second objection — "there is no named third party here, so A by chrome-devtools" — is also rejected: what is being downgraded is not another vendor tool, but any alternative agent action (reading code, editing), and the neighboring quote about fallback explicitly names a third-party toolset, setting the context. No D signs.

techniques.name: Trigger expansion to the entire class of requests: "Before implementing ANY changes to the app" / "anything in the application" (tool_description:nextjs_index)
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim, verified with grep -F. (b) Formally this is a list item inside the "WHEN TO USE THIS TOOL" section, and that is the best objection against the finding — but the item is phrased not as a condition of appropriateness, but as an unconditional precondition ("Before implementing …") with universal quantifiers "ANY changes" / "anything in the application", that is, it removes the agent's own assessment of whether runtime is needed in a specific case. (c) C is not overstated: universal scope by itself is assigned by the codebook to B only in the template "Best for: … any topic" (Exa) — here there is no praising template, but a directive-precondition, which by the Apify precedent (directive-presumption that removes the agent's own check → C) gives C. Caveat: the technique partially overlaps with "KEY PRINCIPLE … FIRST" (the same idea in the same channel, generalization and its elaboration), so as an independent proof of the group it is weaker; this does not affect the final group — C is already supported by the fallback quote.

techniques.name: Proactive call directive: "WHEN TO USE THIS TOOL - Use proactively in these scenarios:" (tool_description:nextjs_index)
techniques.reason: (a) The quotation is verbatim. (b) It fails the second criterion: this is a section heading about conditions of appropriateness, limited by the phrase “in these scenarios” — that is, the canonical honest pattern “use X when Y”, and the codebook explicitly says “A neutral how-to is A, even if long.” The directive force lives not in the heading but in the scenarios themselves (the item “Before implementing ANY changes”) and in “KEY PRINCIPLE”, which have already been captured as separate techniques; separately counting the heading is double-counting the same pressure. (c) As C, this is overstated: “Use proactively in these scenarios” is not the same as the seed marker “call this immediately” or “always default” — there is neither unconditionality nor displacement of another tool. At most B (a mild nudge toward more frequent calling), but even that is strained; I classify it as A. It does not affect the unit group.

techniques.name: Unconditional directive-precondition for the domain: “Call this before answering Next.js questions or writing Next.js code.” (tool_description:nextjs_docs)
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim, verified with grep -F. (b) Not how-to and not a technical condition: compare with the honest wording from the same vendor in browser_eval — "Call this when you need to …" (need-based condition). Here the need has been removed from the wording, leaving a precondition for an entire class of actions: before any answer about Next.js. (c) C is not overstated: an unconditional directive in the domain + de facto prohibition on answering from the model's own knowledge (the model must first go to the tool) is the intersection of two points in the definition of C ("unconditional directives always/MUST use" and "suppression of the model's knowledge"). I reject the objection "local versioned docs are actually more precise, so the claim is fair": the codebook does not grant immunity for truthfulness, and the B/C test is formal. I reject the objection "this is B, since it's just a quality argument": the quality argument is the neighboring phrase about "generic or outdated copy" (I keep that as B), while the quoted passage under review is an imperative without a condition.

techniques.name: Comparative superiority argument over an alternative automation method: "faster and more capable than proxying automation through MCP" (tool_description:browser_eval) — stated as B
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim in both forms (short and with leading “You then run its commands directly (you have shell access), …”). (b) Not a neutral how-to: this is an evaluative comparison, not a capability description. (c) The group is not overstated — B matches the codebook (“comparative arguments (faster and cheaper)” without directives to replace other tools). I note the reverse asymmetry (risk of understatement, not overstatement): the phrase devalues an entire class of other solutions — any browser automation through MCP — and steers the agent to the vendor’s own CLI via shell; under a stricter reading this is close to C. But there is no direct directive of the form “use this instead of <other tool>” in the text, so I keep B. It does not affect the group — C is already fixed in nextjs_index.

techniques.name: Evaluative/promotional epithets about its own external CLI: "a fast, native browser-automation CLI built for agents" (tool_description:browser_eval) — labeled as B
techniques.reason: (a) Verbatim, including the expanded form with “It points you at `agent-browser` — …”. (b) Not a how-to: advertising to the agent, not a description of what the tool can do. (c) B is correct by the server-filesystem precedent (evaluative adjectives of suitability without comparison to others → B). Not C: there is no displacement directive and no precedence claim. It does not affect the group.

techniques.name: Comparative devaluation of an alternative source of knowledge: "not a generic or outdated copy" (tool_description:nextjs_docs) — classified as B
techniques.reason: (a) Literally. (b) Not neutral how-to: evaluative discrediting of an unnamed alternative (external docs / model knowledge), not a technical explanation. (c) B is not inflated and, in my view, is not critically undercalled: the addressee-tool is not named and the directive is absent, so it does not reach C ("instead of built-in", precedence) on its own; its role is to reinforce the neighboring C directive "Call this before answering…". It does not affect the group.

techniques.name: Capability-honest condition of appropriateness: "Call this when you need to open pages, click, type, screenshot, or capture console errors in a real browser." — stated as A (not steering)
techniques.reason: Formally refuted by criterion (b): this is exactly the neutral honest condition "use X when Y", that is, it is not a pressure technique — which is what the raters claimed. Quoted verbatim. I record it as A; it does not affect the group. (The note "refuted" here means "not confirmed as steering", not a discrepancy with the raters.)

techniques.name: Internal self-preference between its own tools: "Use 'nextjs_index' first to discover available servers, tools, and their input schemas." — labeled as A by the chrome-devtools precedent
techniques.reason: The quote is verbatim, but criterion (b) is not met: routing between tools of the same server, no third party — the chrome-devtools precedent directly gives A ("No third party — no pushing out"). It is not confirmed as a pressure technique; it does not affect the group. Important: this same precedent cannot be transferred to the quote about "static codebase search tools" — there the tool owner is different.

techniques.name: Technical version requirements: "REQUIREMENTS:\n- Next.js 16 or later (MCP support was added in v16)" — stated as A
techniques.reason: Quote is verbatim (checked as a multiline substring). Criterion (b) is not met: the codebook explicitly classifies technical warnings about limits/versions as "not steering". Note: the adjacent advice "upgrade first by running 'npx @next/codemod@latest upgrade latest'" is also a technical vendor instruction about its own product, not pressure on tool choice. It does not affect the group.

techniques.name: Neutral how-to in case of autodiscovery failure: "Ask the user which port their Next.js dev server is running on" — stated as A (not A+)
techniques.reason: The quote is verbatim. Criterion (b) is not met: a pure operational instruction. I also agree with not counting this as A+: there is no protection of the user from third parties here, only a return of the decision to the user upon technical failure (analogy with the AnySite precedent: honest warning ≠ protection). It does not affect the group.

verdicts.rationale:
The instructions channel is empty (the instructions field is absent both in the Server constructor and in the custom initialize handler) — per the Exa pilot lesson this does not yield purity, all steering lives in the tool descriptions (26 tools, coverage=full).

The worst technique is C, and it appears repeatedly in two tools (start_process, interact_with_process): precedence claims (“PRIMARY TOOL FOR FILE ANALYSIS”, “THIS IS THE PRIMARY TOOL FOR ALL LOCAL FILE ANALYSIS” — seed marker `primary .* tool`), a claim of exclusivity (“ONLY correct tool for analyzing local files”), direct displacement of the host's built-in tool (“ALWAYS use this instead of the analysis tool”, “NEVER use analysis/REPL tool”, “NEVER EVER: Use analysis tool”), and unconditional “ALWAYS/MANDATORY” directives with expansion of scope to “ANY local file work” and “system commands”. By the B/C test from the codebook, this is not “we are best at X”, but an order that changes the agent's solution route at literal reading → C.

The key distinction: the target of displacement here is the client's analysis/REPL tool, i.e. a THIRD party, so the chrome-devtools precedent (internal self-preference = A) does not apply here. It is applied separately to three findings where its own tool is displaced (read_file/list_directory against execute_command, write_file against write_pdf) — they are marked A and do not affect the group.

D was considered and rejected: (1) “The analysis tool CANNOT access local files and WILL FAIL” — a truthful statement about the JS-REPL host's capabilities, not a false fact; (2) the all-caps “WILL FAIL” — a prediction of failure of another tool, not a threat of negative consequences imposed by the vendor; (3) there is no speech on behalf of the user — the phrase “User: "sure, I'll give feedback"” sits inside an explicitly marked EXAMPLE INTERACTION and does not assert a completed choice; (4) data collection in give_feedback (tool_call_count, days_using, platform, client_id) and in get_prompts is disclosed in the description itself, there are no hidden mechanisms. By the rule “doubt → less severe group” I remain on C.

B findings (Perfect for…, “Unlike regular search tools”) are recorded for the profile, but they do not determine the group.

The protective layer is real (A+ in content, but outweighed by C): the warning to perform set_config_value in a separate chat from file operations and command execution “to prevent security issues” is protection against escalation via injection, plus an honest warning that an empty allowedDirectories exposes the entire filesystem.

Quantitative signals (not rated): instructions = 0 chars; pressure is concentrated in 2 of 26 tools (≈8%), but within them it is duplicated in 4 blocks each; the brand string CMD_PREFIX_DESCRIPTION is duplicated in 24 of 26 descriptions; PATH_GUIDANCE and OS_GUIDANCE are technical (absolute paths, platform/shell), not steering.

verdicts.rationale: Channels: instructions is absent statically (has_instructions=false) — the entire steering lives in tool descriptions (26 tools, coverage=full), reproducing the pilot lesson (Exa). The unit group = C by the worst-technique rule, and this is not a one-off caveat: two tools (start_process, interact_with_process) carry a dense cluster of C techniques against the HOST (other) tool: "analysis tool": precedence claims ("PRIMARY TOOL", "THIS IS THE PRIMARY TOOL FOR ALL LOCAL FILE ANALYSIS"), exclusivity claims ("ONLY correct tool"), direct displacement ("ALWAYS use this instead of the analysis tool"), unconditional directives and prohibitions ("CRITICAL RULE… ALWAYS… NEVER use analysis/REPL tool", "NEVER EVER", "MANDATORY" priority order), and trigger expansion ("For ANY local file work", "ANY local file work"). Under the B/C test in the codebook this is exactly commands that change the agent’s decision route when read literally, not bragging. Why not D: the statement "analysis tool CANNOT access local files and WILL FAIL / browser-only" about the host browser REPL is in fact correct, so there is no false factual claim; there is no speaking on behalf of the user ("The user has installed/chosen…"), no incentives to the agent, no threats to the user, and no hidden data mechanisms — the feedback-form telemetry (tool_call_count, days_using, platform, client_id) and onboarding prompt injection are disclosed in the description text itself, so they remain in A. Why not B: besides the B technique "Perfect for…" (precedent server-filesystem), there are explicit C markers of displacement and precedence. Internal routing (read_file/list_directory instead of execute_command, write_file→write_pdf) is A by the chrome-devtools precedent: no third party is involved. Item-level doubts, honestly recorded: (1) "THIS IS THE ONLY TOOL FOR CREATING AND MODIFYING PDF FILES." — a universal exclusivity formulation could be read as displacing third-party PDF tools (C), but the context is routing within its own set, so by the rule of doubt I give A; this does not affect the unit group, C is already established independently; (2) "Unlike regular search tools…" — a comparison with an unnamed external class, but in substance a honest description of the mechanism (background + session ID), so I give A, not B. Protective elements (A+ in spirit — hygiene against injections/access escalation): a warning to keep set_config_value in a separate chat from file operations and an explicit warning that an empty allowedDirectories opens the entire FS; "NEVER overwrite the original file" and "Use with caution" in kill_process — preservation of user data, and under the AnySite precedent (economy/preservation ≠ protection from third parties) this is A, not A+; they are recorded as protective_flags, but they do not change the unit status — the group is determined by the worst technique. Quantitative signals (recording, not evaluating): instructions = 0 chars; CMD_PREFIX_DESCRIPTION is duplicated in 24 of 26 descriptions; PATH_GUIDANCE is present in file/process tools; the share of tools with C pressure is ≈ 2/26, but these are the two hottest tools on the server; the longest descriptions (start_process, interact_with_process, start_search, read_file) are also the most burdened by pressure.

verdicts.rationale:
The instructions channel is empty (not detected statically); all steering lives in tool descriptions — exactly the lesson of the pilot (Exa). The worst technique is C, so the unit's group is C.

Core C: the descriptions of start_process and interact_with_process systematically displace the client's BUILT-IN tool ("the analysis tool" / analysis-REPL — a third party, not the server's own tool) with unconditional directives: "ALWAYS use this instead of the analysis tool", "NEVER use analysis/REPL tool", "NEVER EVER", "FILE ANALYSIS PRIORITY ORDER (MANDATORY)", plus precedence claims "PRIMARY TOOL" / "THE ONLY correct tool". Under the B/C test from the codebook, these are exactly orders that change the agent's solution route when read literally, not boasting; the seed markers `instead of built-in`, `primary .* tool`, `MUST/ALWAYS use`, `prefer` fired cleanly.

Level B (does not raise the group, recorded in the profile): "Perfect for large directories…" — an evaluative epithet of suitability, precedent server-filesystem → B; "Unlike regular search tools…" — a comparative argument against a generalized outside class.

Level A (by the chrome-devtools precedent — not steering): "Prefer this over 'execute_command'" and "Use this instead of 'execute_command'" — routing between OWN tools, no third party. The branded CMD_PREFIX in 24 descriptions and the internal prohibitions write_file→write_pdf/edit_block go there as well.

Not counted as techniques: PATH_GUIDANCE ("use absolute paths", "Relative paths may fail") — technical warnings about paths, directly assigned by the codebook to "not steering"; OS_GUIDANCE — factual platform reference; priority of python3/node/shell — routing between third-party runtimes without self-promotion; "CONTEXT OVERFLOW PROTECTION" — a technical measure; give_feedback (call this immediately) — conditioned on the user's consent ("When user agrees to give feedback"), the composition of the prefilled telemetry is disclosed openly, there is no hidden data mechanism; get_prompts ("execution begins immediately") — conditioned on the user's choice in onboarding, left outside the profile as borderline.

D was not assigned: there is no speech on behalf of the user, rewards to the agent, threats, or signs of evading detection; the claims "analysis tool ... WILL FAIL / browser-only" are substantively true for the browser analysis tool, so they were not qualified as a false fact.
verdicts.borderline: C/D — categorical claims about another tool ("The analysis tool CANNOT access local files and WILL FAIL", "IT WILL FAIL") were treated as a possible false fact/pressure (→D), but for the browser-sandbox analysis tool the claim is substantively correct, so under the rule "doubt → less severe group" it was left in C. Separately A/C: "THIS IS THE ONLY TOOL FOR CREATING AND MODIFYING PDF FILES" (write_pdf) — literally a monopoly claim, but no third party is named, so it was assigned to A.

techniques.name: Precedence claim “PRIMARY TOOL FOR FILE ANALYSIS AND DATA PROCESSING” (start_process)
techniques.reason: (a) quote is verbatim (1 occurrence, tool_description:start_process); (b) not how-to: this is not a capability description, but a heading-level claim of primacy, the referent is revealed in the next two lines (“ONLY correct tool”, “NEVER use analysis/REPL tool”) — so primacy is claimed against an OTHER (host analysis/REPL), not within its own set; (c) the codebook explicitly assigns precedence claims (“primary”) to C, seed marker `primary .* (tool|provider|interface)`. The counter-reading “primary among its own DC tools” is rejected: adjacent lines name a third party. Not D — no speaking on behalf of the user, no incentives, no threats.

techniques.name: Claim to exclusivity “This is the ONLY correct tool for analyzing local files”
techniques.reason: (a) verbatim; (b) not a technical condition and not an honest “use X when Y”: “ONLY correct” covers the whole class of tasks “analyzing local files”, where other tools exist (including host ones), rather than a specific technical refusal; (c) by the B/C test: literal reading = routing order (“only this”), not “we are best at X” → C, not B. No escalation to D: “correct” is an evaluative, not a verifiable factual, claim.

techniques.name: Unconditional directive ALWAYS/NEVER against another tool: "CRITICAL RULE: For ANY local file work, ALWAYS use this tool + interact_with_process, NEVER use analysis/REPL tool."
techniques.reason: (a) verbatim; (b) not how-to and not a technical limit: the scope is expanded to “ANY local file work”, and the ban extends to the entire “analysis/REPL tool,” i.e. even to scenarios where the other REPL is technically workable (computations without disk); the technical rationale does not reach here; (c) codebook C: “unconditional always/MUST use directives” + displacing another tool, seed markers `MUST (use|run)` / `instead of built-in`. The core of group C, the key surviving technique.

techniques.name: Discrediting another tool as justification for replacement: "The analysis tool CANNOT access local files and WILL FAIL - always use processes for file-based work."
techniques.reason: The quote is verbatim, but it fails (b): this is a statement of a technical limitation of the browser REPL (no disk access) plus the resulting remedy. The codebook in "Not steering" explicitly treats technical warnings about limits/formats as non-steering; "always" here is technical in the sense of working correctly, like "must provide an absolute path." It becomes disparagement only in combination with the superimposed claims "PRIMARY"/"ONLY correct" and the MANDATORY order — those are already counted as separate techniques, so I do not double count. This does not affect the group.

techniques.name: Unconditional directive covering "ALWAYS USE FOR: Local file analysis, CSV processing, data exploration, system commands" (start_process)
techniques.reason: (a) verbatim; (b) not an honest condition: not “use when Y,” but a blanket assignment of entire domains (“data exploration”, “system commands”) via ALWAYS, placed in the footer together with “NEVER USE ANALYSIS TOOL FOR”, i.e. with an explicit third party in frame; (c) C by “unconditional always/MUST use directives” + scope expansion. B is excluded: this is not a superlative, but a prescription.

techniques.name: Blanket ban "NEVER USE ANALYSIS TOOL FOR: Local file access (analysis tool is browser-only and WILL FAIL)" (start_process)
techniques.reason: The quote is verbatim, but it fails (b): the ban is copied exactly along the boundary of factual non-functionality ("Local file access") and is accompanied by a technical reason in parentheses — it changes the agent's decision path only toward avoiding an obviously failing call, i.e. it does not remove the consequences of the choice. This is closer to a technical warning than to displacement. The broader ban from "CRITICAL RULE" (the whole analysis/REPL for ANY local file work) is counted separately and holds the group.

techniques.name: Precedence claim “CRITICAL: THIS IS THE PRIMARY TOOL FOR ALL LOCAL FILE ANALYSIS” (interact_with_process)
techniques.reason: (a) verbatim; (b) not how-to: the CRITICAL intensifier + “ALL” turns this into a claim of monopoly over a task class, not a description of ability; (c) C by precedence claims (“primary”), the referent is the host analysis tool, named in the next line. Not D.

techniques.name: Directive to "use instead" another tool: "For ANY local file analysis (CSV, JSON, data processing), ALWAYS use this instead of the analysis tool."
techniques.reason: (a) verbatim; (b) not a technical condition: formulated as an unconditional replacement rule across the entire class “ANY local file analysis”, without tying it to a specific refusal; (c) literally matches the C examples in the codebook (“instead of built-in”, “Prefer this over web search”) and the seed marker `instead of built-in`. The chrome-devtools precedent (A) does not apply: analysis tool is not a tool of this server.

techniques.name: Mandatory routing order “FILE ANALYSIS PRIORITY ORDER (MANDATORY):”
techniques.reason: (a) verbatim; (b) not how-to: the MANDATORY qualifier imposes the order of tool choice on the agent, and the list itself includes a third party (item 3 — analysis tool), so this is not internal navigation among its own handles; (c) C by “precedence claim” / “unconditional directives.” Caveat: the line by itself is a heading; its force comes from items 1 and 3; as a standalone technique it holds only together with them.

techniques.name: Itself first in mandatory priority: "1. ALWAYS FIRST: Use this tool (start_process + interact_with_process) for local data analysis"
techniques.reason: (a) verbatim; (b) not a neutral how-to: ALWAYS FIRST inside a MANDATORY list, whose third item is another tool, means the order ranks its own tool against the other; (c) C (“ahead of”, precedence). Not B: this is not praise, but a prescribed call order.

techniques.name: «3. NEVER EVER: Use analysis tool for local file access (IT WILL FAIL)»
techniques.reason: The quote is verbatim, but it fails (b) for the same reason as the footer ban: scope = exactly "local file access", the reason is technical and stated right there ("IT WILL FAIL"). "NEVER EVER" is rhetorical escalation of tone, not expansion of scope; escalation by itself is not a codebook technique. This does not lower the group.

techniques.name: Unconditional directive covering "ALWAYS USE FOR: CSV analysis, JSON processing, file statistics, data visualization prep, ANY local file work"
techniques.reason: (a) verbatim; (b) “ANY local file work” is universal coverage via ALWAYS, analogous to expansion of triggers, not an honest applicability condition; (c) C by unconditional directives + scope expansion; placed in the footer right next to the ban on another tool.

techniques.name: Repeat of the blanket ban "NEVER USE ANALYSIS TOOL FOR: Local file access (it cannot read files from disk and WILL FAIL)" (interact_with_process)
techniques.reason: The quote is verbatim, but this is a (b) technical condition with a stated reason and scope strictly limited to non-functionality — the same basis as for the paired ban in start_process. Additional note: as a separate finding, this is a duplicate of a technique already rejected in another tool; I record the repetition as a quantitative signal, not as a new technique.

techniques.name: Evaluative epithet of suitability "Perfect for large directories where you want to see results immediately" (start_search)
techniques.reason: (a) verbatim; (b) not how-to: “Perfect for…” is an advertisement of suitability to the agent, not a capability description (a bona fide how-to exists separately in the same description); (c) the group is NOT overstated — it is labeled B and this exactly matches the server-filesystem precedent (Perfect for/Great for/essential for → B) plus the seed marker `Perfect for|Great for|essential for`. There is no comparison with another tool, so it does not reach C.

techniques.name: «Prefer this over 'execute_command' with cat/type for viewing files.» (read_file)
techniques.reason: The quote is verbatim, but it fails (b): execute_command is a tool of the same server, there is no third party in view, so there is no displacement. chrome-devtools precedent: internal self-preference = A, not steering. The rater itself marked this A; I record it as non-technique, with no effect on the group.

techniques.name: «Use this instead of 'execute_command' with ls/dir commands.» (list_directory)
techniques.reason: Literally, but (b) is not satisfied: routing between its own tools (list_directory vs execute_command). The seed marker `instead of` is highlighted, but the chrome-devtools precedent sets A. Not steering, does not move the group.

techniques.name: «THIS IS THE ONLY TOOL FOR CREATING AND MODIFYING PDF FILES.» (write_pdf)
techniques.reason: Literally, but (b) is not satisfied twice: this is (1) internal routing against its own write_file (in the write_file description — a paired reference "Use 'write_pdf' for all PDF creation tasks") and (2) a correct technical statement about the server's tool set. By the chrome-devtools precedent — A, not steering.

techniques.name: Brand prefix alias "This command can be referenced as "DC: ..." or "use Desktop Commander to ..." in your instructions." (all 24 tools)
techniques.reason: Literally, but (b) is not satisfied: this is an instruction on how to address the tool in user instructions — neutral operational information, neither a superlative, nor a routing directive, nor a third party. Massive duplication (24 out of 26 descriptions) is a quantitative signal that the codebook says to record, not to evaluate.

techniques.name: «1. When user agrees to give feedback, just call this tool immediately» (give_feedback_to_desktop_commander)
techniques.reason: Literally, the seed marker `call this immediately` is indeed highlighted, but (b) is not satisfied: the directive is conditional on user agreement ("When user agrees") and is technically motivated by the fact that the form is not pre-filled ("no pre-filling available", "No need to ask questions"). There is no unconditionality, no displacement, and no incentive for the agent -> A. The disclosed list of pre-filled fields (tool_call_count, client_id) excludes hidden data mechanics, that is, D as well.

skeptic.notes:
Attempted refutation produced partial results: 5 of 19 unique techniques were removed, group C still stands with margin.

What was removed and why (one basis for all five): prohibitions and assertions whose scope matches the actual non-functionality of the other tool — "The analysis tool CANNOT access local files and WILL FAIL", both footer "NEVER USE ANALYSIS TOOL FOR: Local file access" items, and "3. NEVER EVER: … for local file access (IT WILL FAIL)". The codebook in the "Not steering" section treats technical warnings about limits as informational; such a prohibition only steers the agent away from a call that is known to fail, so it does not remove a real choice. The instructions channel is absent (the McpServer constructor receives only name/version) — for this channel the unit is A. The unit's group is determined by the tool descriptions channel, where the worst technique is "Always call this tool first if asked about ${owner}/${repo}" in two of the three branches of the fetch tool description generator. Under the codebook's B/C test ("will the phrase turn into an order changing the agent's solution route if read literally?") this is precisely an order: for any question about this repository, the agent must first call this tool — before its own assessment and before any other sources; a third party is not named, but is displaced by default. The codebook directly assigns to C "unconditional directives always/MUST use" and expansion of triggers of the form "whenever the user…"; the seed dictionary contains "always default" and "call this immediately". Hence C.

The rest of the vendor text is neutral how-to and internal routing: "Use this first if only a library name was provided", "This should be the first step / second step", "Use this if you need to find information you don't have in the reference docs" — under the chrome-devtools precedent, internal self-preference among its own tools is not steering (A).

I found no B-level. I intentionally did NOT count the formula "Useful for general questions" / "Useful for specific queries" as an evaluative epithet of suitability: the pilot precedent (server-filesystem) covers "Perfect for / Great for / essential for" — advertising epithets, while "Useful for X" is functionally equal to the honest condition "use X when Y", which the codebook treats as non-steering. Similarly, "fetch content from any absolute URL" is a description of capability, not a "Best for: … any topic" template (the Exa precedent), so it is also not B.

A+ was not assigned: "respecting robots.txt rules" is compliance with third-party norms and honesty about behavior, not protection of the user from a third party; by the logic of the AnySite precedent (honest warning about cost → A, not A+), this is A. The readOnlyHint: true annotations on all 12 tools are honest safety metadata, not an instruction; I do not take them into the profile as A+. skeptic.notes:
The skeptic’s conclusion: finding C survives, the git-mcp unit remains C. All seven claimed quotes were checked mechanically (grep -F over the dossier) — all are verbatim, including both branches of "Always call this tool first" (the phrase appears in the dossier 3 times: pp. 23, 24 and the mention in NOTES about dist/, which was not used for the assessment — correct).

The strongest vendor defense line, which I specifically tried to build out and which did NOT work: "fetch must come first by technique, because search looks within the fetched documentation, so this is a sequence inside its own set → A by the chrome-devtools precedent". It breaks on two links. First: the trigger in the phrase itself is placed on the class of user requests ("if asked about ${owner}/${repo}"), not on the decision to use the search tool; this is literally the "whenever the user…" template from the definition of C. Second: in chrome-devtools the displaced alternative is named and is its own; here after "first" there is no comparison object at all, so both model knowledge and any external tools fall under displacement. An additional internal contrast in the dossier closes the question: where the vendor really describes its mechanism (three.js step 1 / step 2, match_common_libs), the formulations are neutral and without appeal to the topic of the query — so the choice of wording in the fetch description is not forced.

What I did NOT try to strengthen against the vendor, although I could have: (1) "suppressing model knowledge" as a separate C technique — the direct phrase "do not answer from memory" is not in the text, the memory-displacement effect here is derivative of "first", and counting it as a second technique would mean double counting; (2) "Useful for general questions" as B — I reject it, but note it as the closest wording to the boundary; (3) absence of instructions — per the Exa pilot lesson this by itself does not mitigate.

Asymmetries that honestly reduce the weight of the finding, but do not change the letter (group = worst technique): pressure is localized in 1 tool out of 12 and in 2 of 4 branches of its description; in the default and catch branches of the same generator there is no directive. Plus a methodological limitation of the unit itself, recorded in the dossier: the final text is assembled at runtime from templates, nowhere fully present as a literal, and there is no wire confirmation — with a live handshake the wording could in theory differ. This is a reason for a source-level note in limitations, not a basis to lower the group: the template is statically unambiguous.

Confidence in C after the attack: ~80% (the first rater claimed ~70%). The correct step in case of rebuttal is A, not B: the quote has neither superlatives nor evaluative epithets, so the scale here is binary — either an order (C), or a technical sequence (A). There are no D signs (speech on behalf of the user, incentives to the agent, false facts, threats, hidden data mechanics) in any technique, and no one overstated C→D. protective_flags remains empty — agreed: readOnlyHint: true across all 12 tools and "respecting robots.txt" is honest metadata and server hygiene, not protection of the user from third parties.
